beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Grounded, and four candidates to measure
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: When your sources support a request, the output is grounded.
beats.got: Grounded means the claim can be traced to a real document. Fluent and confident tone says nothing about whether it is true.

beats.trigger: come to about 20% end-to-end: one task in five correct, four in five with a defect, usually where you won't see it.
beats.got: Small error rates compound over a long chain of steps. That is a real argument for why someone has to own the checking.

beats.trigger: Round 1: 10% fabricated → 1% after fix.
beats.got: Checking and fixing in rounds drives errors down fast, on made-up numbers. Fine. I'd like to know who does the fixing.

beats.trigger: Fluency is not evidence, and the model cannot tell you which parts of its output are grounded.
beats.got: Asking the AI 'are you sure?' is not a check. I do this myself, so this is useful to know.

beats.trigger: Run several candidate methods in parallel and measure which one catches what your benchmark says it should.
beats.got: Don't trust one method on reputation. Try several and measure.

beats.trigger: **4. Counter-evidence search.** Look for sources that contradict each claim.

take_homes: 'Are you sure?' is not a check. You need an outside source or test, and someone who owns it.
Pick a quality check by trying a few on your own material and keeping the one that scores best. Then write down what it can't catch.
Agent proposes, a person checks, then it acts. A human expert stays in the loop where the cost of an error is high.

monday.move: Pick one HR output that goes out under my name, like a policy answer or a people-metrics summary. Ask my team which claims in it are traceable to a source. Then take 'agent proposes, expert checks, then it acts' to the leadership team as my answer on roles, instead of yes or no on headcount.
monday.who: Me, plus one HR business partner
monday.when: Monday, in the weekly HR leadership slot
monday.stop_condition: If the data involved is employee data, I stop and ask the works council and the DPO first.
monday.blocker: I haven't spoken to the works council or the DPO. I also don't have a Module 3 briefing I trust enough to test, and I'm not sure I can build the judge file without a technical colleague.

misconception.why: Nothing said directly that headcount is safe. But the checking work (an expert reviews the proposal, the evidence and the check's limits) is a new kind of work, and the module shows an agent being trusted only a rung at a time. So 'which roles go' now looks like the wrong question to me. 'Which checks and whose judgment do we need' looks better. I'm not convinced yet.

one_line: The middle was agents testing agents and I tuned out, but the point that a human must check what the AI proposes, with the checker's limits written down, is what I'm taking to my leadership team.
